data.content:
## When this skill applies

The user's message contains `website_url:` followed by a URL, e.g.

```
website_url: https://www.example.com/product/analytics
```

or they ask in prose to clone / replicate / rebuild a specific live page. Either
way, run the procedure below. There is no separate confirmation step: the
`website_url:` prefix *is* the instruction.

Deliverable: a new subfolder of the **current workspace** containing a Next.js +
TypeScript app that reproduces that one page as faithfully as a careful human
front-end engineer would — layout, type, colour, spacing, entrance animations,
scroll behaviour, canvas/Rive/Lottie graphics, carousels, and responsive
behaviour from 320px to 2560px — with every asset self-hosted so the page makes
**zero remote requests**.

---

## Step 0 — Load memory first (mandatory)

Before touching anything, load both scopes. This is what stops you rediscovering
the same gotchas every run.

1. `read_memory({ scope: 'global', topic: 'Website replica lessons' })` — durable
   cross-site gotchas (renderer-build mismatches, sanitizer traps, cascade
   ordering, font hosting, viewport quirks). If it doesn't exist yet, note that
   and continue.
2. `list_memory({ scope: 'project' })`, then read any note whose title mentions
   replicas, scraping, this skill, or the target domain. A previous run's
   **note** on the same site is the single most valuable thing you can find —
   the note, never that run's code (see "Never build from another run" below).

Apply what you learn — if the global note says "always check the Rive renderer
build", check it *this* run, don't rediscover it.

---

## Step 1 — Derive the folder slug

Strict, deterministic rule:

1. Strip the scheme and any leading `www.`.
2. Drop the query string and hash entirely.
3. Remove **every** non-alphanumeric character (dots, slashes, hyphens,
   underscores all vanish).
4. Lowercase.
5. Append `-1`. If `<slug>-1` already exists in the workspace, try `-2`, `-3`, …
   and use the first free one. Never reuse or overwrite an existing folder.

| Input URL | Folder |
|---|---|
| `https://url.com/page` | `urlcompage-1` |
| `https://www.foo-bar.com/a/b?x=1` | `foobarcomab-1` |
| `https://example.com/` | `examplecom-1` |
| `https://example.com` (taken) | `examplecom-2` |

Verify with `glob` before creating.

---

## Step 2 — Copy the template

The vendored template lives beside this skill:

```
~/.klenny/skills/website-replica/template/
```

Copy the whole tree into `<workspace>/<slug>/`. On Windows/Git Bash:

```bash
mkdir -p "<slug>" && cp -r ~/.klenny/skills/website-replica/template/. "<slug>/"
```

Then fill in the placeholders (use `edit_file`, never shell substitution):

- `package.json` — `__SLUG__` → the slug; `__TARGET_URL__` → the URL.
- `README.md` — `__SLUG__`, `__TARGET_URL__`, `__PORT__`.

Never edit the template in-place for a specific site. If you discover a genuine
**general** improvement, fix the template too — but do it as a separate,
deliberate edit, and say so in your summary.

The pristine template and the folder you are creating are the **only** code you
may read this run — see the next section.

---

## Never build from another run in this repo (hard requirement)

The workspace may already contain replicas from earlier runs — `examplecom-1`,
`examplecom-2`, a half-finished attempt, or a different site entirely. Treat
every one of them as off-limits for the whole run:

- **Do not read** another replica folder's source — no `read_file`, `grep`,
  `glob`, `codebase_search`, or shell `cat` into `<other-slug>/**`. The only
  code you may open is the pristine
  `~/.klenny/skills/website-replica/template/` and the folder you are building
  right now.
- **Do not copy** files, components, CSS, `replica.config.json` values, effect
  modules, or `ClientRuntime.tsx` wiring out of another run.
- **Do not** diff your output against another run, or use one to "check" your
  work.

Exactly two inputs are legitimate: **memory notes** (Step 0) and **this run's
own capture of the live site** (`scrape/**` and the `app/generated/**` your own
pipeline produced). Every line you write must be justified by what this run
actually observed on the target page.

Why this is a hard rule and not a preference: a neighbouring replica is a
plausible-looking but unverified answer to a *different* question. Copying from
it silently imports that run's assumptions — its fade-in active class, its Rive
renderer build, its stripped-class list, its port, its section names — none of
which were derived from *this* URL. That converts a capture-driven replica into
a guess that merely compiles, and the resulting defects are precisely the kind
that clear every gate and surface only as "it doesn't quite look right".
Knowledge is supposed to travel between runs through memory notes, which are
written deliberately and reviewed; code is not.

If you find yourself wanting a neighbour's file, the correct move is to re-read
this run's `scrape/analysis/**` and look at the live page again.

---

## Step 3 — Write `replica.config.json`

Copy `replica.config.example.json` → `replica.config.json` and set at minimum:

```json
{
  "targetUrl": "https://www.example.com/product/analytics",
  "slug": "examplecomproductanalytics",
  "port": 3300
}
```

Pick a port unlikely to collide (3300+). Everything else has defaults in
`scripts/lib/config.mjs`; only add keys when a site actually needs them. This
file is the **only** place site-specific knowledge belongs — never hardcode a
URL, selector, or class name into a script.

---

## Step 4 — Install and run the pipeline

```bash
cd "<slug>" && npm install
npm run pipeline     # capture → scrape → extras → analyze → codegen
```

Chromium comes from the cached `ms-playwright` install via `playwright-core`. If
`scripts/lib/chromium.mjs` reports it missing, run the install command it prints
(`npx playwright install chromium`) and retry.

Then **read the artifacts before writing any code** — this is the recon step that
determines whether the replica is faithful or merely approximate:

| File | What to look for |
|---|---|
| `scrape/features.json` | Which libraries and effect classes the page actually uses. |
| `scrape/runtime-requirements.json` | Exact library + version to `npm i`, and the suggested command. |
| `scrape/analysis/summary.json` | Section census, data-attribute census, inline script/style dumps. |
| `app/generated/manifest.json` | Sections emitted, stylesheet cascade order, asset counts, sanitizer stats. |

The sanitizer stats matter: if `strippedClasses` is empty on an obviously
animated page, the strip list is wrong for this site and every entrance
animation will ship frozen. Add the real class names to
`codegen.stripClasses` and re-run `npm run codegen`.

### `captureMode` — which markup codegen builds from (read this)

The capture writes **two** HTML files, and choosing wrong causes a whole class
of visible duplication bugs:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `scrape/raw/index.static.html` | The pre-JS server response. Pristine. |
| `scrape/raw/index.html` | The **rendered** DOM after the page's JS ran. |

A rendered capture contains whatever the site's own JS had already *done*:
clone nodes appended into containers, headings split into per-word spans,
absolutely-positioned overlay clones left mid-animation. **Stripping runtime
classes and inline styles does not remove those — they are nodes, not state.**
They then ship as permanent copies *and* get regenerated at runtime, so the
replica renders animated elements twice. Worse, the sanitizer strips the
`opacity: 0` that was keeping a transient clone invisible, so a clone the real
site never shows becomes permanently visible.

`captureMode` (top level of `replica.config.json`) controls the source:

- `"auto"` (default) — uses the static file when it has ≥70% as many elements
  as the rendered DOM, else falls back to rendered. Right for nearly every
  server-rendered site (Webflow, WordPress, Framer, Astro, Next SSG).
- `"static"` — always use the pre-JS response. Best when you have confirmed
  the site is server-rendered.
- `"rendered"` — always use the rendered DOM. Necessary for genuine
  client-rendered SPAs where the static file is an empty shell.

Codegen prints the choice and the ratio every run; check that line. If it used
`rendered` on a site you believe is server-rendered, investigate before
building on top of it.

When you are stuck on `rendered` (real SPA), two config-driven escape hatches
remove baked runtime nodes generically:

- `codegen.emptySelectors` — elements that are pure **hosts** for runtime
  children (a clone container). Shipped childless and stripped of inline
  `style`.
- `codegen.unwrapSelectors` — runtime-generated **wrappers** around authored
  content (per-word/per-letter split spans, typewriter carets). Replaced by
  their own children, restoring the pristine text so the site's JS can re-split
  it at runtime.

Both default to a marker attribute only (`[data-replica-empty]` /
`[data-replica-unwrap]`), so they are inert until you name real selectors.

---

## Step 5 — Tune `app/ClientRuntime.tsx`

This is the one file you are expected to hand-edit. The captured markup is inert;
this is where the page comes back to life.

1. Enable the effects `features.json` says the site uses. The pure-DOM ones
   (fade-in, nav toggle/scroll/dropdown, tabs, accordion, counters, marquee,
   lazy images, forms, smooth anchors) are already listed and self-disable when
   their targets are absent.
2. Fix the fade-in active class if the site's isn't `faded-in`:
   `createFadeIn({ activeClass: 'is-visible' })`. Get the real name from the
   captured CSS — guessing here is the #1 cause of an invisible page.
3. For library-backed effects, install the exact detected version, then
   uncomment the adapter line:
   - `createCarousel({ load: () => import('swiper/bundle') })`
   - `createRive({ load: () => import('@rive-app/webgl2') })` — **the renderer
     build must match what the site used**; a webgl2 `.riv` renders blank under
     `@rive-app/canvas` with no error at all.
   - `createLottie({ load: () => import('lottie-web') })`
4. Add site-specific effects as new modules in `app/lib/`, keeping the
   `EffectInit` contract (no-op without targets, return a teardown, idempotent
   under React strict mode).

### Beware: the sanitizer strips `webflow.js`, and it was suppressing clicks

Webflow widget controls are anchors whose href names an element to *reveal*, not
a place to scroll: a tab link is `<a href="#w-tabs-0-data-w-pane-0" role="tab">`,
and lightbox/dropdown triggers have the same shape. On the live site `webflow.js`
binds these and calls `preventDefault()`. The sanitizer drops `webflow.js`, so in
the replica **nothing suppresses that href any more**. Two failure modes follow,
and they are easy to miss because neither logs an error:

1. **A generic smooth-anchor effect will bind them.** `initSmoothAnchors` now
   excludes `.w-tab-link, [role="tab"], [data-w-tab], [aria-controls]`,
   `[data-tab], .w-dropdown-toggle, .w-lightbox, [data-fancybox]`. Keep that
   exclusion list in sync if you add widget effects.
2. **Any handler you hand-write for a widget control must call
   `preventDefault()` itself** to stand in for the `webflow.js` that no longer
   exists, or the browser performs native fragment navigation.

This is nastier than a normal cosmetic bug because carousel/tab autoplay scripts
routinely synthesise `tab.click()` on a timer (coframe.com fires one every 4s).
Either failure mode then re-scrolls the page to that widget *forever*, so a
reader who scrolls past it is dragged back every few seconds and effectively
cannot read the rest of the page. Nothing in `tsc`, the unit tests, or the
viewport gate catches it — the page is structurally perfect and simply refuses to
stay scrolled.

**How to check:** with the section's autoplay confirmed *armed* (park on it until
the active tab advances on its own — the `IntersectionObserver` usually needs it
50% visible), scroll well past it, wait through 3+ autoplay ticks, then assert
`window.scrollY` has not moved and `location.hash` is still empty. Verifying from
a cold jump past the section proves nothing: autoplay never armed, so the timer
that causes the bug never ran.

---

## Step 6 — The verification gate (all of it, in order)

Everything below must pass. Do not report success on a partial gate.

```bash
npm run verify      # tsc --noEmit + vitest + next build, all clean
npm run viewports   # 7-viewport browser audit — must exit 0
```

`npm run viewports` gates on: horizontal overflow, oversized elements, the
burger/desktop nav swap, canvas backing-store and paint state, animation trigger
counts pre/post scroll, carousel init, broken images, console errors, failed
requests, **duplicated visible headings**, and **any remote (non-self-hosted)
request**.

The `duplicate-visible-text` check is the gate for the baked-runtime-node bug
described under `captureMode` in Step 4. It tallies `h1/h2/h3` text and flags
any string rendered **visibly more than once**, walking ancestors for
`display`/`visibility`/`opacity` so transient clones parked at `opacity: 0`
(which real sites legitimately keep in the DOM) do not false-positive. If the
live site genuinely shows duplicate headings, baseline it in
`replica.baseline.json` under `duplicateVisibleText` per viewport.

Then the side-by-side visual comparison:

```bash
npm run dev &       # server must be up for the local screenshots
npm run compare     # writes [local | live | diff] composites per viewport
```

Read the composites with `read_image` and actually look at them. **A non-zero
diff percentage is expected** — A/B-tested copy, live counters, cookie banners
and font rasterization all differ between runs. Judge *where* the diff is
concentrated: 0.4% spread evenly is fine, 0.4% concentrated in the hero is a real
bug. Iterate until the remaining diff is explainable, and say in your summary
what remains and why.

If the live site itself overflows or has a layout quirk, record it in
`replica.baseline.json` rather than "fixing" it. A replica that fixes the
original's bugs is no longer a replica.

### Definition of done

- `tsc --noEmit` clean.
- `next build` clean.
- Generated vitest suite green.
- 7/7 viewports pass (`npm run viewports` exits 0).
- Zero broken images, zero remote requests, zero console errors.
- Zero duplicated visible headings beyond what live itself shows.
- **Verify duplication against the live site, in the browser, not by counting
  nodes.** Element/attribute counts are not evidence: the site's own JS creates
  transient clones, so a raw count differs from live for entirely correct
  reasons. Measure whether text is *visibly* rendered twice, run the identical
  measurement on the live page, and treat live as the arbiter. Also check the
  live DOM, not just generated JSX — codegen and the runtime port can each
  produce this symptom independently.
- Side-by-side comparison screenshots produced, reviewed, and any residual
  difference explained.

---

## Step 7 — Tear everything down

Before writing your final message:

- Stop the dev server (kill the background `next dev`; confirm the port is free).
- Close every browser window/tab the pipeline or your own `browser` tool calls
  opened. Nothing should be left running.

---

## Step 8 — Write memory (mandatory, both scopes)

1. **Project scope** — a per-site note titled e.g.
   `Website replica — example.com/product/analytics`, covering: the URL and
   folder slug; the port; libraries installed and why; the exact
   `replica.config.json` overrides needed; which effects were enabled and any
   custom active-class names; every bug hit and its fix; the final gate results
   and residual visual diff; anything a future run against this same site should
   know first.
2. **Global scope** — append genuinely **cross-site** lessons to
   `Website replica lessons`. Read it first and merge; never clobber it. Only
   durable, transferable knowledge belongs here (a new runtime-artifact class
   worth stripping by default, a font-hosting trap, a renderer-build mismatch) —
   site-specific trivia stays in the project note.

If you improved the vendored template, record that in the global note too.

Write both notes as if the folder you just built will be **unreadable** to your
successor — because under the rule above, it will be. Anything a future run
needs must be stated *in the note*, not left to be inferred from the code.

---

## Step 9 — Final message requirements

The last message must include, explicitly:

1. The exact command to launch the server, with the directory:
   ```bash
   cd <slug> && npm run dev
   ```
2. The localhost URL **including the port**: `http://localhost:3300`
3. The full gate results (typecheck / build / tests / viewports / visual diff).
4. Any residual visual difference and why it's acceptable.
5. Confirmation that the dev server and browser windows were shut down.
6. Which memory notes you wrote.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never** read or copy code from another replica folder in this workspace.
  Memory notes and this run's own capture are the only legitimate inputs (see
  "Never build from another run in this repo").
- **Never** hardcode site-specific values into `scripts/**`. They stay
  URL-agnostic; site knowledge lives in `replica.config.json`.
- **Never** hand-edit `app/generated/**` — codegen overwrites it. Fix the config
  or the generator instead.
- **Never** reorder the CSS `@import` list. Cascade order is load-bearing and
  reordering silently breaks layout in ways that are painful to debug.
- **Never** let a form POST to the original endpoint. `app/lib/forms.ts`
  intercepts submissions locally; keep it that way.
- Single page only. Internal links are rewritten to absolute live-site URLs;
  in-page `#anchors` stay local.
- Use `read_file`/`edit_file`/`write_file`/`multi_write` for all file authoring.
  Shell redirection into files is blocked on Windows.

   - `createRive({ load: () => import('@rive-app/webgl2') })` — **the renderer
     build must match what the site used**; a webgl2 `.riv` renders blank under
     `@rive-app/canvas` with no error at all.
   - `createLottie({ load: () => import('lottie-web') })`
4. Add site-specific effects as new modules in `app/lib/`, keeping the
   `EffectInit` contract (no-op without targets, return a teardown, idempotent
   under React strict mode).

### Beware: the sanitizer strips `webflow.js`, and it was suppressing clicks

Webflow widget controls are anchors whose href names an element to *reveal*, not
a place to scroll: a tab link is `<a href="#w-tabs-0-data-w-pane-0" role="tab">`,
and lightbox/dropdown triggers have the same shape. On the live site `webflow.js`
binds these and calls `preventDefault()`. The sanitizer drops `webflow.js`, so in
the replica **nothing suppresses that href any more**. Two failure modes follow,
and they are easy to miss because neither logs an error:

1. **A generic smooth-anchor effect will bind them.** `initSmoothAnchors` now
   excludes `.w-tab-link, [role="tab"], [data-w-tab], [aria-controls]`,
   `[data-tab], .w-dropdown-toggle, .w-lightbox, [data-fancybox]`. Keep that
   exclusion list in sync if you add widget effects.
2. **Any handler you hand-write for a widget control must call
   `preventDefault()` itself** to stand in for the `webflow.js` that no longer
   exists, or the browser performs native fragment navigation.

This is nastier than a normal cosmetic bug because carousel/tab autoplay scripts
routinely synthesise `tab.click()` on a timer (coframe.com fires one every 4s).
Either failure mode then re-scrolls the page to that widget *forever*, so a
reader who scrolls past it is dragged back every few seconds and effectively
cannot read the rest of the page. Nothing in `tsc`, the unit tests, or the
viewport gate catches it — the page is structurally perfect and simply refuses to
stay scrolled.

**How to check:** with the section's autoplay confirmed *armed* (park on it until
the active tab advances on its own — the `IntersectionObserver` usually needs it
50% visible), scroll well past it, wait through 3+ autoplay ticks, then assert
`window.scrollY` has not moved and `location.hash` is still empty. Verifying from
a cold jump past the section proves nothing: autoplay never armed, so the timer
that causes the bug never ran.

---

## Step 6 — The verification gate (all of it, in order)

Everything below must pass. Do not report success on a partial gate.

```bash
npm run verify      # tsc --noEmit + vitest + next build, all clean
npm run viewports   # 7-viewport browser audit — must exit 0
```

`npm run viewports` gates on: horizontal overflow, oversized elements, the
burger/desktop nav swap, canvas backing-store and paint state, animation trigger
counts pre/post scroll, carousel init, broken images, console errors, failed
requests, **duplicated visible headings**, and **any remote (non-self-hosted)
request**.

The `duplicate-visible-text` check is the gate for the baked-runtime-node bug
described under `captureMode` in Step 4. It tallies `h1/h2/h3` text and flags
any string rendered **visibly more than once**, walking ancestors for
`display`/`visibility`/`opacity` so transient clones parked at `opacity: 0`
(which real sites legitimately keep in the DOM) do not false-positive. If the
live site genuinely shows duplicate headings, baseline it in
`replica.baseline.json` under `duplicateVisibleText` per viewport.

Then the side-by-side visual comparison:

```bash
npm run dev &       # server must be up for the local screenshots
npm run compare     # writes [local | live | diff] composites per viewport
```

Read the composites with `read_image` and actually look at them. **A non-zero
diff percentage is expected** — A/B-tested copy, live counters, cookie banners
and font rasterization all differ between runs. Judge *where* the diff is
concentrated: 0.4% spread evenly is fine, 0.4% concentrated in the hero is a real
bug. Iterate until the remaining diff is explainable, and say in your summary
what remains and why.

If the live site itself overflows or has a layout quirk, record it in
`replica.baseline.json` rather than "fixing" it. A replica that fixes the
original's bugs is no longer a replica.

### Definition of done

- `tsc --noEmit` clean.
- `next build` clean.
- Generated vitest suite green.
- 7/7 viewports pass (`npm run viewports` exits 0).
- Zero broken images, zero remote requests, zero console errors.
- Zero duplicated visible headings beyond what live itself shows.
- **Verify duplication against the live site, in the browser, not by counting
  nodes.** Element/attribute counts are not evidence: the site's own JS creates
  transient clones, so a raw count differs from live for entirely correct
  reasons. Measure whether text is *visibly* rendered twice, run the identical
  measurement on the live page, and treat live as the arbiter. Also check the
  live DOM, not just generated JSX — codegen and the runtime port can each
  produce this symptom independently.
- Side-by-side comparison screenshots produced, reviewed, and any residual
  difference explained.

---

## Step 7 — Tear everything down

Before writing your final message:

- Stop the dev server (kill the background `next dev`; confirm the port is free).
- Close every browser window/tab the pipeline or your own `browser` tool calls
  opened. Nothing should be left running.

---

## Step 8 — Write memory (mandatory, both scopes)

1. **Project scope** — a per-site note titled e.g.
   `Website replica — example.com/product/analytics`, covering: the URL and
   folder slug; the port; libraries installed and why; the exact
   `replica.config.json` overrides needed; which effects were enabled and any
   custom active-class names; every bug hit and its fix; the final gate results
   and residual visual diff; anything a future run against this same site should
   know first.
2. **Global scope** — append genuinely **cross-site** lessons to
   `Website replica lessons`. Read it first and merge; never clobber it. Only
   durable, transferable knowledge belongs here (a new runtime-artifact class
   worth stripping by default, a font-hosting trap, a renderer-build mismatch) —
   site-specific trivia stays in the project note.

If you improved the vendored template, record that in the global note too.

Write both notes as if the folder you just built will be **unreadable** to your
successor — because under the rule above, it will be. Anything a future run
needs must be stated *in the note*, not left to be inferred from the code.

---

## Step 9 — Final message requirements

The last message must include, explicitly:

1. The exact command to launch the server, with the directory:
   ```bash
   cd <slug> && npm run dev
   ```
2. The localhost URL **including the port**: `http://localhost:3300`
3. The full gate results (typecheck / build / tests / viewports / visual diff).
4. Any residual visual difference and why it's acceptable.
5. Confirmation that the dev server and browser windows were shut down.
6. Which memory notes you wrote.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never** read or copy code from another replica folder in this workspace.
  Memory notes and this run's own capture are the only legitimate inputs (see
  "Never build from another run in this repo").
- **Never** hardcode site-specific values into `scripts/**`. They stay
  URL-agnostic; site knowledge lives in `replica.config.json`.
- **Never** hand-edit `app/generated/**` — codegen overwrites it. Fix the config
  or the generator instead.
- **Never** reorder the CSS `@import` list. Cascade order is load-bearing and
  reordering silently breaks layout in ways that are painful to debug.
- **Never** let a form POST to the original endpoint. `app/lib/forms.ts`
  intercepts submissions locally; keep it that way.
- Single page only. Internal links are rewritten to absolute live-site URLs;
  in-page `#anchors` stay local.
- Use `read_file`/`edit_file`/`write_file`/`multi_write` for all file authoring.
  Shell redirection into files is blocked on Windows.

# Website replica lessons (cross-site, durable)

Read this **before** running the `website-replica` skill (`~/.klenny/skills/website-replica/`).
Only genuinely transferable knowledge belongs here — site-specific trivia goes in the
per-project note. Merge into this file; never clobber it.

Origin: generalized from the `coframe3` replica in `C:\all\projects\CoframeTakehome`
(the reference implementation this template was built from) plus its project memory notes.

## The single biggest trap: rendered-DOM capture bakes in runtime state

Capturing the **rendered** DOM (necessary for SPAs) means the page's JavaScript has already
run and mutated it. That mutation is invisible in a screenshot but fatal in codegen:

- Runtime classes: `faded-in`, `aos-animate`, `is-inview`, `swiper-initialized`,
  `swiper-slide-active`, `w--current`, `is-loaded`, `splitting`.
- Runtime inline styles: `opacity`, `transform`, `transition`, `visibility`, `will-change`.

Ship those as-is and every entrance animation renders **already finished** — or worse, frozen
at `opacity: 0`, so entire sections are invisible with no error anywhere. Hence:

1. Codegen sanitizes them out (`codegen.stripClasses` / `stripInlineStyleProps`).
2. `app/ClientRuntime.tsx` re-applies them at the right moment.
3. `tests/generated.test.ts` fails the build if any survive.

**If `manifest.json`'s `sanitizer.strippedClasses` is empty on an obviously animated page,
the strip list is wrong for that site.** Find the real class names in the captured CSS and add
them to config. Do not assume the defaults covered it.

### Runtime **nodes** are the other half of this trap — and stripping can't reach them

Classes and inline styles are *state*; a rendered capture also contains whole **nodes** the
site's JS created: clones appended into containers, headings split into per-word/per-letter
spans, absolutely-positioned overlay clones left mid-animation. No amount of class/style
stripping removes a node. They ship as permanent duplicates **and** get regenerated at runtime,
so the replica renders the same element twice.

The nastiest variant: a transient clone the real site keeps invisible at `opacity: 0` gets
baked in, then the sanitizer strips `opacity` (it's in the strip list) while leaving
`position`/`z-index` (which aren't) — so a clone the original **never shows** becomes
permanently visible on top of real content. That was the coframe.com `coframecom-2` bug:
12 `cloneContent()` overlays at `z-index:9999`, 2 cursor clones, 10 split hero spans.

**Fix it at the source, not with more stripping:** `captureMode` (`'auto'|'static'|'rendered'`)
selects which HTML codegen builds from. `auto` (the default) uses the pristine pre-JS
`index.static.html` whenever it has >=70% as many elements as the rendered DOM, which is right
for essentially every server-rendered site (Webflow/WordPress/Framer/Astro/Next SSG). Only a
genuine client-rendered SPA needs `rendered`. Codegen prints the choice and the ratio — read
that line. Setting `static` on coframe.com (ratio 0.82) eliminated all baked runtime nodes at
a stroke.

When genuinely stuck on `rendered`, two config-driven passes remove them generically:
`codegen.emptySelectors` (ship a runtime-clone **host** childless) and
`codegen.unwrapSelectors` (replace a runtime **wrapper** with its own children, restoring
pristine text so the site's script can re-split it). Both are inert until you name selectors.
Note these two alone were **not sufficient** on coframe.com — they can only remove what you
thought to enumerate; `captureMode` removes the entire category.

### Duplication must be measured as *visible* text, against live

This cost me a full wrong diagnosis: after the fix, local still reported
"12 overlay clones, 6 duplicate headings", so I concluded the fix had failed and invented a
nonexistent "runtime port bug" in the ported cursor module. Running the **identical** script
against live coframe.com returned byte-identical numbers. Real sites legitimately keep
transient invisible clones in the DOM permanently.

- Raw node/attribute/element counts are **not evidence** of a duplication bug.
- Measure whether a string is *visibly* rendered more than once, walking ancestors for
  `display:none` / `visibility:hidden` / `opacity <= 0.05`.
- Run the same measurement on the live page and let **live be the arbiter** (same rule as the
  `--live` baseline discipline below).
- Check the **live runtime DOM**, not just the generated JSX — codegen and the runtime port can
  each produce this symptom independently, so clean JSX alone doesn't prove a clean render.
- The template's viewport audit now gates on this as `duplicate-visible-text`, baselined per
  viewport via `replica.baseline.json` -> `duplicateVisibleText`.

Corollary: the fade-in "finished state" class is **not** always `faded-in`. Guessing it is the
#1 cause of a blank-looking replica. Read the CSS, then pass the real one:
`createFadeIn({ activeClass: 'is-visible' })`.

### The sanitizer also strips styles an effect then has to re-establish

Stripping is not free: it can delete the *initial* state as well as the finished one. A control
captured mid-interaction with inline `opacity:0; display:none` comes out of codegen with **no**
inline style, and if its CSS rule says `display:flex` it now starts **visible**. Any module that
owns that element's choreography must therefore apply the "hidden at start" step itself at init,
before its async runtime resolves, or the control flashes over the content on first paint.
Check the *generated* JSX for the element, not the raw capture, before assuming what survived.

## Capture pre-scroll for markup, post-scroll for assets

These two needs conflict, so the pipeline does both passes:

- **Markup source = pre-scroll DOM.** Least runtime mutation baked in.
- **Asset discovery = network log from the post-scroll pass.** Catches lazy-loaded images and
  runtime-fetched fonts/wasm.

coframe3 hardcoded a font family (Inter) to work around this; the network-log approach makes
that unnecessary and generic. Never hardcode a font/library name again — read the network log.

## URL rewriting has TWO distinct paths — fix both or fonts silently 404

Learned the hard way on rust-lang.org (all 7 viewports failed):

- **Markup attributes** go through `localAsset()`, which absolutises relative refs against the
  page URL, so root-relative `src="/static/x.png"` resolves fine.
- **CSS text** went through a *substring* replacer that only matched FULL absolute URLs. Real
  stylesheets overwhelmingly use `url(/static/fonts/x.woff2)` (root-relative) or
  `url(../fonts/x.woff2)` (sheet-relative), which never match an absolute asset-map key.

Result: 180 font files downloaded correctly into `public/assets/fonts/`, and *every single one*
still 404'd at runtime because the vendored CSS kept pointing at the original site's paths.
Fixed by `rewriteCssUrls(text, baseUrl)` which parses `url()` / `@import` and resolves each ref
through `localAsset()` — with the **stylesheet's own URL** as the base, not the page URL, or
`../` refs land one directory too high. It reports a `css url() localised` count and warns on
unmapped refs; a zero count on a page with webfonts means this pass isn't running.

Note the *warning* itself is not a gate: a "N css url() refs could not be mapped" message is
often a false positive (e.g. refs inside `@font-face` blocks whose files are all present on
disk). Spot-check a few of the named files in `public/assets/` and let **runtime 404s** be the
arbiter, not the warning count.

## Match `www.`/apex host aliases in the asset map

Sites routinely declare markup on one host and serve from the other (rust-lang.org declares
`<link rel=icon href="https://rust-lang.org/...">` while the page is `https://www.rust-lang.org/`).
Exact-key asset-map lookups miss on that alias alone, so a file **already downloaded** looks
missing. `localAsset()` now tries both directions. Symptom: an asset visibly present in
`public/assets/` that codegen claims it can't map.

## Icons must be local-or-dropped, never local-or-remote

`<link rel=icon>` variants are **real subresource fetches on every page load** (unlike
`og:`/`twitter:` images, which are crawler-only metadata and may stay absolute). Falling back
to the remote URL when an icon isn't in the asset map leaks cross-origin requests and breaks the
offline guarantee. Scrape only downloads what the browser actually requested, so icon variants
for other DPRs/platforms are routinely absent — drop those, don't keep them remote.

Related: **Chromium probes `/favicon.ico` at the origin root regardless of declared icons.**
That probe is issued by the *browser process*, so it never appears in Playwright's page-level
`request`/`response` events — it surfaces only as an unattributable console 404 with an empty
`failedRequests` list. Diagnostic tell: the same single 404 appears at *every* viewport and the
dev-server log shows no 404 at all. `fetch-extras.mjs` fetches upstream `/favicon.ico`, and if
upstream doesn't serve one (rust-lang.org 301s to an apex 404), copies the best local icon
there instead. Affects no rendered pixel — it just silences a phantom 404 and fixes the tab icon.

## Disable the Next.js dev indicator before trusting any visual diff

`next dev` renders a dev badge in the bottom-left corner on every page. The live site has
nothing there, so it registers as a permanent local-only delta at *every* viewport — inflating
the diff and, far worse, **masking real regressions in that corner**. `devIndicators: false`
in `next.config.mjs` took example.com from 0.21% avg (with a 4.56% worst band) to a clean 0.00%.
Any nonzero floor that appears identically at all 7 viewports is an artifact, not a fidelity gap.

## Renderer build must match (Rive, and anything wasm-backed)

A `.riv` exported for **webgl2** renders completely blank under `@rive-app/canvas` — no
exception, no console error, just an empty canvas. Same class of failure for webgl vs canvas2d
builds of other libraries.

- Get the build from the CDN URL in the network log (`fetch-extras.mjs` distinguishes
  webgl2/webgl/canvas and reports it in `runtime-requirements.json`).
- Self-host the `.wasm` and point the loader at it (`RuntimeLoader.setWasmUrl`), or the page
  silently fetches from unpkg at runtime and breaks the zero-remote-requests guarantee.
- Call `resizeDrawingSurfaceToCanvas()` on load, or the canvas backing store mismatches its CSS
  box and the animation renders blurry / wrongly scaled. Worth checking the backing store
  explicitly in the viewport audit — a blank-but-present canvas passes every naive check.
- **The `data-*` config attributes may live on a WRAPPER element, not the `<canvas>` itself.**
  The generic adapter's `canvas[data-rive-url]` selector then matches nothing and the animation
  never mounts, silently. Check where the attribute actually sits and select the host, then
  `.querySelector('canvas')` inside it.

## Webflow IX2 sites: the animation data is in a JS chunk, not the CSS

On Webflow pages, `webflow.js` is stripped as a third-party script, which silently removes an
entire class of animation. Tell-tale: an element that visibly moves on the live site but has
**no `@keyframes` and no `animation` property** anywhere in the captured CSS, often with a
captured inline `transform: translate3d(...)` + `will-change: transform` (i.e. caught
mid-flight) and a `data-w-id` attribute.

Do not invent replacement timings — they're recoverable exactly. Grep the captured
`webflow.schunk.*.js` for the element's `data-w-id`; you'll find an `actionLists` entry with
titled action groups and precise `config` values (`duration`, `delay`, `xValue`, `easing`,
`actionTypeId`, and `useFirstGroupAsInitialState`). Port those numbers verbatim. `PLUGIN_RIVE`
action items carry the state-machine input to fire (e.g. `inputs: { onRestart: true }` — handle
both trigger-shaped `fire()` and boolean-shaped `value = true`, since the payload is ambiguous).

Marquee-specific: IX2 marquees typically animate `0% → -50%` over a fixed duration against
markup that **already contains two copies** of the strip, so -50% wraps seamlessly. The
template's generic clone-based `initMarquee` must be dropped for these — cloning a third set
desynchronises the wrap. Beware how wide `[class*="marquee"]` reaches: on one site it matched
five nested classes, so the generic effect would have cloned children of all of them.

## CSS cascade order is load-bearing

Rebuild stylesheets in **exact `<head>` document order** (`vendor-NN-*.css`, `inline-NN.css`,
then a pure `@import` list in `index.css`). Reordering or "tidying" them changes specificity
outcomes and silently breaks layout in ways that are miserable to debug. Never hand-sort.
`tests/generated.test.ts` asserts the `@import` list matches `manifest.json.stylesheets` order.

Note `manifest.stylesheets` is a plain filename array of *successfully emitted* sheets, so it
can be compared to the `@import` list directly; sheets that failed to localise carry a `status`
instead of a `file`, are excluded from both, and are reported as a warning. Richer per-sheet
metadata (order/kind/bytes/remainingRemote) lives in `stylesheetDetails`.

## Don't fix the original's bugs — but verify "upstream does it too" before baselining

Live sites frequently have real horizontal overflow or layout quirks at some viewport. A
replica that fixes them is no longer a replica, and it fails a strict diff *worse*. Record them
in `replica.baseline.json` as tolerated known-upstream quirks and move on.

**But confirm parity first with `--live` rather than reasoning about it.** On rust-lang.org
`curl` showed `/favicon.ico` 301→404 upstream, which looked like "the original 404s too, so
baseline it" — then `viewport-check --live` showed LIVE passing `ok` while local failed. The
inference was wrong and baselining would have hidden a genuine local-only defect. The `--live`
run is one command; use it as the arbiter every time.

This applies to *repeat* runs of a site you've already replicated, too: a quirk documented in a
previous run's memory note is a hypothesis, not evidence. Re-measure it live this run before
writing it into the baseline. Compare the full metric set (overflowBy, scrollWidth,
scrollHeight, and the top `tooWide` culprit) — matching on all four is what makes it credible,
and it's worth recording those numbers *in* the baseline file so the next run can audit it.

Faithfulness cuts both ways: upstream's own dead code should stay dead. If a captured script's
hover-pause handler targets a selector that matches nothing (e.g. `.swiper-wrapper` when that
Swiper declares a custom `wrapperClass`), reproduce the no-op rather than "fixing" it into
behaviour the original never had. Note it in the project memory instead.

## Non-zero visual diff is normal — read *where*, not *how much*

A/B-tested copy, live counters, cookie banners, and font rasterization differ run to run.
0.4% spread evenly is fine; 0.4% concentrated in the hero is a real bug. That's why
`compare-live.mjs` emits a 10-band worst-region breakdown alongside the headline number, and
`[local | live | diff]` composites — actually `read_image` them. A composite caught the dev-badge
artifact above that the headline percentage alone made look like harmless noise.

Page height delta is the cheapest strong signal: identical `local NNNNpx / live NNNNpx` across
all viewports means the layout genuinely reflowed the same way, not just that pixels averaged out.

On pages with long-running animations (a 10s chart, a 25s marquee, randomised cursor labels),
expect a stubborn ~1% floor that is pure **motion phase**: both sides are correct, caught at
different frames. Recognise it by *what* differs — diff confined inside a canvas, or doubled
logo/text ghosts — versus the real-bug signature of solid blocks and shifted edges. Height
parity alongside it is the confirmation.

## Block third-party noise at capture time

Analytics/consent/chat hosts inject DOM that isn't part of the design and pollutes both the
capture and the diff. Block by host during capture (`blockHosts`) and/or drop by selector
(`codegen.dropSelectors`). Cheaper than deleting the nodes afterwards.

## Never POST to the original endpoint

Captured forms point at someone else's CRM. `app/lib/forms.ts` intercepts submissions, toggles
the site's own success/error state locally, and logs instead. Keep it that way — a replica
sending real leads to the original owner is a genuine harm, not a cosmetic issue.

The same rule covers **redirects**, not just POSTs: a hero "analyze my site" form whose handler
navigates to the product's real signup host must be intercepted too. Preserve the validation,
blocklists and alert copy exactly, and stop only at the side effect.

## Effect-module contract that survives contact with real sites

Every effect: no-op silently when targets are absent, return a teardown, be idempotent under
React strict mode (which double-mounts in dev — the marquee cloner needs an explicit
`data-marquee-cloned` guard or it duplicates twice). `initEffects()` isolates throwing effects
so one bad selector can't blank the page.

Keep the template dependency-free: pure-DOM effects implemented outright, library-backed ones
(Swiper/Rive/Lottie) as adapters taking a `load: () => import(...)` callback. This keeps
`tsc`/`next build` green with nothing extra installed and degrades a missing library to a
logged warning instead of a crash.

**Exactly one owner per behaviour.** If a module both registers itself in `ClientRuntime` *and*
gets called from inside a sibling module's init, it initialises twice: two handler sets, two
competing timers each with its own state, and the inner call's teardown discarded (leaked
timer). Symptom is maddening — a control that won't stay selected because the other closure's
timer overwrites it. When delegating a port to a subagent, state explicitly that it must not
call sibling init functions internally.

Ported scripts often ran on `DOMContentLoaded` / `window.load`. By the time a React effect
mounts, `DOMContentLoaded` has **already fired**, so re-registering that listener means the code
never runs. Run it immediately, and for load-gated work use
`document.readyState === 'complete' ? run() : addEventListener('load', run, { once: true })`.
Where an async runtime is involved, trigger from its own `onLoad` instead.

Watch for self-feeding observers: a callback that writes to the element its ResizeObserver /
MutationObserver watches will loop forever and hang the page (and the Playwright harness) with
no error. Memoize the last written values and bail early when unchanged.

## Verification that actually catches things

Beyond tsc/build/tests, the browser audit gates on: horizontal overflow, oversized elements,
burger/desktop nav swap at the breakpoint, canvas backing-store *and* paint state, animation
trigger counts pre/post scroll, carousel init, broken images, console errors, failed requests,
and **any remote request at all**. The last one is what keeps "self-hosted" honest over time.

Assertions must not over-constrain: `assets.total > 0` and `stylesheets.length > 0` are wrong,
because a page with no external sub-resources or no CSS is a legitimate, fully-replicated page.
Assert the *reconciliation* (per-kind counts sum to the total; `@import` list equals the manifest
list) instead of a magnitude. Also scan `metadata.ts` for remote origins, not just `.tsx`/`.css` —
that gap is exactly how the remote-icon leak survived a green test run.

**Smoke-test on a content-rich site, never a trivial one.** example.com (1 section, 0 assets,
1 inline sheet) passed every gate while three separate real bugs sat in the pipeline; rust-lang.org
(197 elements, 8 sections, 219 assets, 2 webfont families, 4 stylesheets) surfaced all of them
within one run. A trivial target exercises neither the splitter, nor the cascade rebuild, nor the
asset downloader.

### Don't sample a moving value across two tool calls

Seconds of real time elapse between a `browser` click and the follow-up `inspect`. If a 4s
autoplay timer is mutating the thing you're reading, the second call returns a *different*
moment — and reading it as the click's result invents bugs that don't exist. This cost two
speculative "fixes" on one run before the misdiagnosis was caught.

Assert an **invariant** that holds at every instant instead of an exact expected value:
`activeTab === activePane`, `location.hash === ''`, `scrollY` drift `=== 0`,
`getAnimations().length === 1`. Those are true regardless of when the sample lands.

Also: **Playwright's click does its own scroll-into-view**, which shows up as a one-off `scrollY`
change that looks exactly like a page-side autoscroll bug. Distinguish them by clicking a second
already-visible element — harness-caused drift goes to 0, a real anchor hijack keeps firing.

### Verify a negative grep before acting on it

# Website replica lessons (cross-site, durable)

Read this **before** running the `website-replica` skill (`~/.klenny/skills/website-replica/`).
Only genuinely transferable knowledge belongs here — site-specific trivia goes in the
per-project note. Merge into this file; never clobber it.

Origin: generalized from the `coframe3` replica in `C:\all\projects\CoframeTakehome`
(the reference implementation this template was built from) plus its project memory notes.

## The single biggest trap: rendered-DOM capture bakes in runtime state

Capturing the **rendered** DOM (necessary for SPAs) means the page's JavaScript has already
run and mutated it. That mutation is invisible in a screenshot but fatal in codegen:

- Runtime classes: `faded-in`, `aos-animate`, `is-inview`, `swiper-initialized`,
  `swiper-slide-active`, `w--current`, `is-loaded`, `splitting`.
- Runtime inline styles: `opacity`, `transform`, `transition`, `visibility`, `will-change`.

Ship those as-is and every entrance animation renders **already finished** — or worse, frozen
at `opacity: 0`, so entire sections are invisible with no error anywhere. Hence:

1. Codegen sanitizes them out (`codegen.stripClasses` / `stripInlineStyleProps`).
2. `app/ClientRuntime.tsx` re-applies them at the right moment.
3. `tests/generated.test.ts` fails the build if any survive.

**If `manifest.json`'s `sanitizer.strippedClasses` is empty on an obviously animated page,
the strip list is wrong for that site.** Find the real class names in the captured CSS and add
them to config. Do not assume the defaults covered it.

### Runtime **nodes** are the other half of this trap — and stripping can't reach them

Classes and inline styles are *state*; a rendered capture also contains whole **nodes** the
site's JS created: clones appended into containers, headings split into per-word/per-letter
spans, absolutely-positioned overlay clones left mid-animation. No amount of class/style
stripping removes a node. They ship as permanent duplicates **and** get regenerated at runtime,
so the replica renders the same element twice.

The nastiest variant: a transient clone the real site keeps invisible at `opacity: 0` gets
baked in, then the sanitizer strips `opacity` (it's in the strip list) while leaving
`position`/`z-index` (which aren't) — so a clone the original **never shows** becomes
permanently visible on top of real content. That was the coframe.com `coframecom-2` bug:
12 `cloneContent()` overlays at `z-index:9999`, 2 cursor clones, 10 split hero spans.

**Fix it at the source, not with more stripping:** `captureMode` (`'auto'|'static'|'rendered'`)
selects which HTML codegen builds from. `auto` (the default) uses the pristine pre-JS
`index.static.html` whenever it has >=70% as many elements as the rendered DOM, which is right
for essentially every server-rendered site (Webflow/WordPress/Framer/Astro/Next SSG). Only a
genuine client-rendered SPA needs `rendered`. Codegen prints the choice and the ratio — read
that line. Setting `static` on coframe.com (ratio 0.82) eliminated all baked runtime nodes at
a stroke.

When genuinely stuck on `rendered`, two config-driven passes remove them generically:
`codegen.emptySelectors` (ship a runtime-clone **host** childless) and
`codegen.unwrapSelectors` (replace a runtime **wrapper** with its own children, restoring
pristine text so the site's script can re-split it). Both are inert until you name selectors.
Note these two alone were **not sufficient** on coframe.com — they can only remove what you
thought to enumerate; `captureMode` removes the entire category.

### Duplication must be measured as *visible* text, against live

This cost me a full wrong diagnosis: after the fix, local still reported
"12 overlay clones, 6 duplicate headings", so I concluded the fix had failed and invented a
nonexistent "runtime port bug" in the ported cursor module. Running the **identical** script
against live coframe.com returned byte-identical numbers. Real sites legitimately keep
transient invisible clones in the DOM permanently.

- Raw node/attribute/element counts are **not evidence** of a duplication bug.
- Measure whether a string is *visibly* rendered more than once, walking ancestors for
  `display:none` / `visibility:hidden` / `opacity <= 0.05`.
- Run the same measurement on the live page and let **live be the arbiter** (same rule as the
  `--live` baseline discipline below).
- Check the **live runtime DOM**, not just the generated JSX — codegen and the runtime port can
  each produce this symptom independently, so clean JSX alone doesn't prove a clean render.
- The template's viewport audit now gates on this as `duplicate-visible-text`, baselined per
  viewport via `replica.baseline.json` -> `duplicateVisibleText`.

Corollary: the fade-in "finished state" class is **not** always `faded-in`. Guessing it is the
#1 cause of a blank-looking replica. Read the CSS, then pass the real one:
`createFadeIn({ activeClass: 'is-visible' })`.

### The sanitizer also strips styles an effect then has to re-establish

Stripping is not free: it can delete the *initial* state as well as the finished one. A control
captured mid-interaction with inline `opacity:0; display:none` comes out of codegen with **no**
inline style, and if its CSS rule says `display:flex` it now starts **visible**. Any module that
owns that element's choreography must therefore apply the "hidden at start" step itself at init,
before its async runtime resolves, or the control flashes over the content on first paint.
Check the *generated* JSX for the element, not the raw capture, before assuming what survived.

## Capture pre-scroll for markup, post-scroll for assets

These two needs conflict, so the pipeline does both passes:

- **Markup source = pre-scroll DOM.** Least runtime mutation baked in.
- **Asset discovery = network log from the post-scroll pass.** Catches lazy-loaded images and
  runtime-fetched fonts/wasm.

coframe3 hardcoded a font family (Inter) to work around this; the network-log approach makes
that unnecessary and generic. Never hardcode a font/library name again — read the network log.

## URL rewriting has TWO distinct paths — fix both or fonts silently 404

Learned the hard way on rust-lang.org (all 7 viewports failed):

- **Markup attributes** go through `localAsset()`, which absolutises relative refs against the
  page URL, so root-relative `src="/static/x.png"` resolves fine.
- **CSS text** went through a *substring* replacer that only matched FULL absolute URLs. Real
  stylesheets overwhelmingly use `url(/static/fonts/x.woff2)` (root-relative) or
  `url(../fonts/x.woff2)` (sheet-relative), which never match an absolute asset-map key.

Result: 180 font files downloaded correctly into `public/assets/fonts/`, and *every single one*
still 404'd at runtime because the vendored CSS kept pointing at the original site's paths.
Fixed by `rewriteCssUrls(text, baseUrl)` which parses `url()` / `@import` and resolves each ref
through `localAsset()` — with the **stylesheet's own URL** as the base, not the page URL, or
`../` refs land one directory too high. It reports a `css url() localised` count and warns on
unmapped refs; a zero count on a page with webfonts means this pass isn't running.

Note the *warning* itself is not a gate: a "N css url() refs could not be mapped" message is
often a false positive (e.g. refs inside `@font-face` blocks whose files are all present on
disk). Spot-check a few of the named files in `public/assets/` and let **runtime 404s** be the
arbiter, not the warning count.

## Match `www.`/apex host aliases in the asset map

Sites routinely declare markup on one host and serve from the other (rust-lang.org declares
`<link rel=icon href="https://rust-lang.org/...">` while the page is `https://www.rust-lang.org/`).
Exact-key asset-map lookups miss on that alias alone, so a file **already downloaded** looks
missing. `localAsset()` now tries both directions. Symptom: an asset visibly present in
`public/assets/` that codegen claims it can't map.

## Icons must be local-or-dropped, never local-or-remote

`<link rel=icon>` variants are **real subresource fetches on every page load** (unlike
`og:`/`twitter:` images, which are crawler-only metadata and may stay absolute). Falling back
to the remote URL when an icon isn't in the asset map leaks cross-origin requests and breaks the
offline guarantee. Scrape only downloads what the browser actually requested, so icon variants
for other DPRs/platforms are routinely absent — drop those, don't keep them remote.

Related: **Chromium probes `/favicon.ico` at the origin root regardless of declared icons.**
That probe is issued by the *browser process*, so it never appears in Playwright's page-level
`request`/`response` events — it surfaces only as an unattributable console 404 with an empty
`failedRequests` list. Diagnostic tell: the same single 404 appears at *every* viewport and the
dev-server log shows no 404 at all. `fetch-extras.mjs` fetches upstream `/favicon.ico`, and if
upstream doesn't serve one (rust-lang.org 301s to an apex 404), copies the best local icon
there instead. Affects no rendered pixel — it just silences a phantom 404 and fixes the tab icon.

## Disable the Next.js dev indicator before trusting any visual diff

`next dev` renders a dev badge in the bottom-left corner on every page. The live site has
nothing there, so it registers as a permanent local-only delta at *every* viewport — inflating
the diff and, far worse, **masking real regressions in that corner**. `devIndicators: false`
in `next.config.mjs` took example.com from 0.21% avg (with a 4.56% worst band) to a clean 0.00%.
Any nonzero floor that appears identically at all 7 viewports is an artifact, not a fidelity gap.

## Renderer build must match (Rive, and anything wasm-backed)

A `.riv` exported for **webgl2** renders completely blank under `@rive-app/canvas` — no
exception, no console error, just an empty canvas. Same class of failure for webgl vs canvas2d
builds of other libraries.

- Get the build from the CDN URL in the network log (`fetch-extras.mjs` distinguishes
  webgl2/webgl/canvas and reports it in `runtime-requirements.json`).
- Self-host the `.wasm` and point the loader at it (`RuntimeLoader.setWasmUrl`), or the page
  silently fetches from unpkg at runtime and breaks the zero-remote-requests guarantee.
- Call `resizeDrawingSurfaceToCanvas()` on load, or the canvas backing store mismatches its CSS
  box and the animation renders blurry / wrongly scaled. Worth checking the backing store
  explicitly in the viewport audit — a blank-but-present canvas passes every naive check.
- **The `data-*` config attributes may live on a WRAPPER element, not the `<canvas>` itself.**
  The generic adapter's `canvas[data-rive-url]` selector then matches nothing and the animation
  never mounts, silently. Check where the attribute actually sits and select the host, then
  `.querySelector('canvas')` inside it.

## Webflow IX2 sites: the animation data is in a JS chunk, not the CSS

On Webflow pages, `webflow.js` is stripped as a third-party script, which silently removes an
entire class of animation. Tell-tale: an element that visibly moves on the live site but has
**no `@keyframes` and no `animation` property** anywhere in the captured CSS, often with a
captured inline `transform: translate3d(...)` + `will-change: transform` (i.e. caught
mid-flight) and a `data-w-id` attribute.

Do not invent replacement timings — they're recoverable exactly. Grep the captured
`webflow.schunk.*.js` for the element's `data-w-id`; you'll find an `actionLists` entry with
titled action groups and precise `config` values (`duration`, `delay`, `xValue`, `easing`,
`actionTypeId`, and `useFirstGroupAsInitialState`). Port those numbers verbatim. `PLUGIN_RIVE`
action items carry the state-machine input to fire (e.g. `inputs: { onRestart: true }` — handle
both trigger-shaped `fire()` and boolean-shaped `value = true`, since the payload is ambiguous).

Marquee-specific: IX2 marquees typically animate `0% → -50%` over a fixed duration against
markup that **already contains two copies** of the strip, so -50% wraps seamlessly. The
template's generic clone-based `initMarquee` must be dropped for these — cloning a third set
desynchronises the wrap. Beware how wide `[class*="marquee"]` reaches: on one site it matched
five nested classes, so the generic effect would have cloned children of all of them.

## CSS cascade order is load-bearing

Rebuild stylesheets in **exact `<head>` document order** (`vendor-NN-*.css`, `inline-NN.css`,
then a pure `@import` list in `index.css`). Reordering or "tidying" them changes specificity
outcomes and silently breaks layout in ways that are miserable to debug. Never hand-sort.
`tests/generated.test.ts` asserts the `@import` list matches `manifest.json.stylesheets` order.

Note `manifest.stylesheets` is a plain filename array of *successfully emitted* sheets, so it
can be compared to the `@import` list directly; sheets that failed to localise carry a `status`
instead of a `file`, are excluded from both, and are reported as a warning. Richer per-sheet
metadata (order/kind/bytes/remainingRemote) lives in `stylesheetDetails`.

## Don't fix the original's bugs — but verify "upstream does it too" before baselining

Live sites frequently have real horizontal overflow or layout quirks at some viewport. A
replica that fixes them is no longer a replica, and it fails a strict diff *worse*. Record them
in `replica.baseline.json` as tolerated known-upstream quirks and move on.

**But confirm parity first with `--live` rather than reasoning about it.** On rust-lang.org
`curl` showed `/favicon.ico` 301→404 upstream, which looked like "the original 404s too, so
baseline it" — then `viewport-check --live` showed LIVE passing `ok` while local failed. The
inference was wrong and baselining would have hidden a genuine local-only defect. The `--live`
run is one command; use it as the arbiter every time.

This applies to *repeat* runs of a site you've already replicated, too: a quirk documented in a
previous run's memory note is a hypothesis, not evidence. Re-measure it live this run before
writing it into the baseline. Compare the full metric set (overflowBy, scrollWidth,
scrollHeight, and the top `tooWide` culprit) — matching on all four is what makes it credible,
and it's worth recording those numbers *in* the baseline file so the next run can audit it.

Faithfulness cuts both ways: upstream's own dead code should stay dead. If a captured script's
hover-pause handler targets a selector that matches nothing (e.g. `.swiper-wrapper` when that
Swiper declares a custom `wrapperClass`), reproduce the no-op rather than "fixing" it into
behaviour the original never had. Note it in the project memory instead.

## Non-zero visual diff is normal — read *where*, not *how much*

A/B-tested copy, live counters, cookie banners, and font rasterization differ run to run.
0.4% spread evenly is fine; 0.4% concentrated in the hero is a real bug. That's why
`compare-live.mjs` emits a 10-band worst-region breakdown alongside the headline number, and
`[local | live | diff]` composites — actually `read_image` them. A composite caught the dev-badge
artifact above that the headline percentage alone made look like harmless noise.

Page height delta is the cheapest strong signal: identical `local NNNNpx / live NNNNpx` across
all viewports means the layout genuinely reflowed the same way, not just that pixels averaged out.

On pages with long-running animations (a 10s chart, a 25s marquee, randomised cursor labels),
expect a stubborn ~1% floor that is pure **motion phase**: both sides are correct, caught at
different frames. Recognise it by *what* differs — diff confined inside a canvas, or doubled
logo/text ghosts — versus the real-bug signature of solid blocks and shifted edges. Height
parity alongside it is the confirmation.

## Block third-party noise at capture time

Analytics/consent/chat hosts inject DOM that isn't part of the design and pollutes both the
capture and the diff. Block by host during capture (`blockHosts`) and/or drop by selector
(`codegen.dropSelectors`). Cheaper than deleting the nodes afterwards.

## Never POST to the original endpoint

Captured forms point at someone else's CRM. `app/lib/forms.ts` intercepts submissions, toggles
the site's own success/error state locally, and logs instead. Keep it that way — a replica
sending real leads to the original owner is a genuine harm, not a cosmetic issue.

The same rule covers **redirects**, not just POSTs: a hero "analyze my site" form whose handler
navigates to the product's real signup host must be intercepted too. Preserve the validation,
blocklists and alert copy exactly, and stop only at the side effect.

## Effect-module contract that survives contact with real sites

Every effect: no-op silently when targets are absent, return a teardown, be idempotent under
React strict mode (which double-mounts in dev — the marquee cloner needs an explicit
`data-marquee-cloned` guard or it duplicates twice). `initEffects()` isolates throwing effects
so one bad selector can't blank the page.

Keep the template dependency-free: pure-DOM effects implemented outright, library-backed ones
(Swiper/Rive/Lottie) as adapters taking a `load: () => import(...)` callback. This keeps
`tsc`/`next build` green with nothing extra installed and degrades a missing library to a
logged warning instead of a crash.

**Exactly one owner per behaviour.** If a module both registers itself in `ClientRuntime` *and*
gets called from inside a sibling module's init, it initialises twice: two handler sets, two
competing timers each with its own state, and the inner call's teardown discarded (leaked
timer). Symptom is maddening — a control that won't stay selected because the other closure's
timer overwrites it. When delegating a port to a subagent, state explicitly that it must not
call sibling init functions internally.

Ported scripts often ran on `DOMContentLoaded` / `window.load`. By the time a React effect
mounts, `DOMContentLoaded` has **already fired**, so re-registering that listener means the code
never runs. Run it immediately, and for load-gated work use
`document.readyState === 'complete' ? run() : addEventListener('load', run, { once: true })`.
Where an async runtime is involved, trigger from its own `onLoad` instead.

Watch for self-feeding observers: a callback that writes to the element its ResizeObserver /
MutationObserver watches will loop forever and hang the page (and the Playwright harness) with
no error. Memoize the last written values and bail early when unchanged.

## Verification that actually catches things

Beyond tsc/build/tests, the browser audit gates on: horizontal overflow, oversized elements,
burger/desktop nav swap at the breakpoint, canvas backing-store *and* paint state, animation
trigger counts pre/post scroll, carousel init, broken images, console errors, failed requests,
and **any remote request at all**. The last one is what keeps "self-hosted" honest over time.

Assertions must not over-constrain: `assets.total > 0` and `stylesheets.length > 0` are wrong,
because a page with no external sub-resources or no CSS is a legitimate, fully-replicated page.
Assert the *reconciliation* (per-kind counts sum to the total; `@import` list equals the manifest
list) instead of a magnitude. Also scan `metadata.ts` for remote origins, not just `.tsx`/`.css` —
that gap is exactly how the remote-icon leak survived a green test run.

**Smoke-test on a content-rich site, never a trivial one.** example.com (1 section, 0 assets,
1 inline sheet) passed every gate while three separate real bugs sat in the pipeline; rust-lang.org
(197 elements, 8 sections, 219 assets, 2 webfont families, 4 stylesheets) surfaced all of them
within one run. A trivial target exercises neither the splitter, nor the cascade rebuild, nor the
asset downloader.

### Don't sample a moving value across two tool calls

Seconds of real time elapse between a `browser` click and the follow-up `inspect`. If a 4s
autoplay timer is mutating the thing you're reading, the second call returns a *different*
moment — and reading it as the click's result invents bugs that don't exist. This cost two
speculative "fixes" on one run before the misdiagnosis was caught.

Assert an **invariant** that holds at every instant instead of an exact expected value:
`activeTab === activePane`, `location.hash === ''`, `scrollY` drift `=== 0`,
`getAnimations().length === 1`. Those are true regardless of when the sample lands.

Also: **Playwright's click does its own scroll-into-view**, which shows up as a one-off `scrollY`
change that looks exactly like a page-side autoscroll bug. Distinguish them by clicking a second
already-visible element — harness-caused drift goes to 0, a real anchor hijack keeps firing.

### Verify a negative grep before acting on it

A grep that finds nothing is weak evidence, because the pattern may simply be wrong. A

# coframecom-2 — 5th coframe.com replica run (port 3301)

Slug `coframecom-2` (coframecom-1 was taken). All gates green:
`tsc` clean, **34/34** vitest, `next build` 4/4 pages, **7/7** viewports,
compare-live avg **1.15%**.

## Findings NEW to this run (not in the earlier coframe notes)

### 1. Logo marquee is Webflow IX2, NOT a CSS animation
There are **zero `@keyframes`** for the marquee in the captured CSS. Movement
comes from IX2 action list `"a"` ("Logo Animation") on
`data-w-id="674d6aa7-c193-2fe4-61dd-3519f496b39e"`
(`.logo-marquee__animation-container`), and `webflow.js` is stripped:

| group | xValue | duration | meaning              |
|-------|--------|----------|----------------------|
| 1     | 0%     | 500      | initial state        |
| 2     | -50%   | 25000    | the scroll           |
| 3     | 0%     | 0        | instant loop restart |

Ported with `element.animate()`, 25000ms, `iterations: Infinity`, linear.
The captured markup **already contains 2 logo sets**, so -50% wraps
seamlessly. **Never clone** — and the template's generic `initMarquee` must be
dropped, because `[class*="marquee"]` matches FIVE nested classes here
(`.logo-marquee`, `__animation-container`, `__logos`, `__logo`, `__logo-item`)
and would clone children of all of them.

### 2. Rive replay-button choreography = IX2 `a-4` "Play Chart Animation"
| group | delay | action |
|-------|-------|--------|
| 1 | 0     | GENERAL_DISPLAY `none` + STYLE_OPACITY `0` on `.impact__replay-button` |
| 2 | 100   | PLUGIN_RIVE → State Machine input `onRestart` |
| 3 | 10000 | GENERAL_DISPLAY `flex` + STYLE_OPACITY `1` |

`script-29.js` fires the first play with `replayButton.click()` on
DOMContentLoaded → initial play and replay are the SAME code path. Since the
React module mounts long after DOMContentLoaded, trigger the sequence from
Rive's `onLoad` instead, and gate clicks on a `loaded` flag.

**Codegen strips the replay button's inline `opacity:0;display:none`**, and
`.impact__replay-button` is `display:flex` in CSS → it starts VISIBLE. The
module must apply group 1 at init or the button sits over the chart at first
paint. (I initially asserted the inline style survived — it does not.)

### 3. `data-rive-url` is on the wrapper DIV, canvas is its child
Template's default `canvas[data-rive-url]` matches nothing → chart never
mounts. Use `[data-rive-url]` then `.querySelector('canvas')`. Attributes to
honour: `data-rive-state-machine="State Machine"`, `data-rive-artboard`,
`data-rive-fit="contain"`, `data-rive-alignment="center"`.

### 4. GREP GOTCHA that nearly caused a wrong "fix"
`.nav-dropdown.visible` rules are **tab-indented inside media queries**. A
pattern like `'[^}{,]*\.visible[^{,]*{[^}]*}'` (excluding commas/newlines)
finds nothing, and I briefly concluded the CSS was missing and that script-17's
class toggles couldn't work. Correct check: `grep -oh '[^{}]*\.visible[^{}]*{'`.
The rules exist; the class-toggle port is right. **Verify a negative grep with
a second, looser pattern before acting on it.**

### 5. Duplicate tab-engine init (real bug, subagent-authored)
`initCoframeSwipers` called `initCoframeIntroTabs(root)` internally *and*
ClientRuntime registered it as its own effect → tab engine initialised TWICE:
two click-handler sets, two competing 4s autoplay timers each with its own
`currentTab`, and the inner call's teardown discarded (leaked timer). Removed
the inner call. **When delegating a port, tell the subagent not to call sibling
init functions internally if the runtime registers them separately.**

### 6. Intro Swiper cannot slide; hover-pause is dead upstream
`slidesPerView: '3'` with exactly 3 slides → `allowSlideNext: false`,
`realIndex` pinned at 0. Tabs are the real control. Also
`swiperTabsContainer` targets `.introduction.swiper .swiper-wrapper` but this
Swiper's `wrapperClass` is `introduction__steps`, so hover-pause matches
nothing — **same dead selector in upstream `script-28.js`**, so it was left
faithful.

### 7. ipad-pro +27px re-verified live this run
Local vs live identical: `overflowBy 27`, `scrollWidth 1051` (innerWidth 1024),
`scrollHeight 12931`, same top culprit `div.cursor-container` (w=1051,
right=1051). Recorded in `replica.baseline.json`. Replica was *cleaner* than
live: 0 console errors / 0 failed / 0 remote vs live's 2 errors + 10 failed.
`#cursor-container`'s baked inline `width:1440px;height:12586px` still must be
cleared once at init, and ResizeObserver writes memoized or it self-feeds.

## Verification-method lesson (cost me two bogus "fixes")
Autoplay advances a tab every 4s; several seconds elapse between a `browser`
click call and the follow-up `inspect` call. Reading `activeTab` across two
round-trips and treating it as static made me "diagnose" a broken tab click
twice. **Never treat a value sampled across separate tool calls as static when
a timer mutates it** — assert an invariant instead. Here the real invariant
(`activeTab === activePane`, `hash === none`, `scrollY` drift 0) held in every
single sample.

Also: Playwright's click does its own scroll-into-view, which produced a 44px
one-off `scrollY` change. Proved it was the harness by clicking a second time
(drift 0), not the page.

## Autoscroll regression: PASS
17s unattended at the Introduction section → `scrollY` 1243→1243 (drift **0**),
`location.hash` `(none)`, tabs advanced 2→1 (autoplay alive), marquee
`getAnimations().length === 1` (no strict-mode double-init).

# coframecom-2 — "page shows duplicated elements" bug (root cause + fix)

## Symptom the user reported
A static "coframe" arrow bubble sitting next to the animated one, the hero-ish
line "What if your website optimized itself?" appearing twice / frozen instead
of animating, and other doubled headings.

## Root cause (ONE bug, at codegen — not two)
`scripts/codegen.mjs` built the JSX from the **rendered** capture
(`scrape/raw/index.html`), which contains nodes coframe's own JS had already
created after load:

1. `.cursor-container` with 2 baked `.cursor` clones (`data-should-reset="true"`).
2. Hero `<h1>` split into 10 `.letter-effect` spans by `fadeInText()`.
3. **12 `cloneContent()` overlay clones** across 6 sections
   (`position:absolute; opacity:0; z-index:9999; transition:none`).

The sanitizer only stripped runtime **classes** and **inline style props** — it
never removed runtime-generated **nodes**. Worse, `opacity` and `transition` are
in the strip list but `position`/`z-index` are not, so clone #3 shipped with its
invisibility removed → a permanently visible duplicate of real copy.

## The fix that actually worked: `captureMode: "static"`
`captureMode` was a **declared but unimplemented** config option (defaulted to
`'rendered'`, never read by codegen). Implemented it in `codegen.mjs` +
`scripts/lib/config.mjs` as `'auto' | 'static' | 'rendered'`:
- `auto` (new default) picks `index.static.html` when
  `staticCount/renderedCount >= 0.7`, else falls back to rendered (safe for SPAs).
- This project sets `"captureMode": "static"` explicitly (coframe.com is
  Webflow = fully server-rendered; ratio measured 0.82, 1176 vs 1439 elements,
  and the static file contains every structural piece at identical counts).

Result: generated JSX has **0** occurrences of `zIndex:"9999"`,
`data-should-reset`, `letter-effect`, `thin-cursor`.

## Also added (generic escape hatches, for when stuck on `rendered`)
- `codegen.emptySelectors` — ships matched elements childless + strips inline
  style (used here for `.cursor-container`).
- `codegen.unwrapSelectors` — replaces matched elements with their own children
  (used here for `.letter-effect`).

These were implemented FIRST and were **not sufficient** on their own — they
missed the 12 z-index:9999 overlay clones, which is what led to finding
`captureMode`. Both are still in `replica.config.json` and still correct.

## Regression gate added
`scripts/viewport-check.mjs` now has a `duplicate-visible-text` check: tallies
`h1/h2/h3` text, flags any string rendered **visibly more than once**, walking
ancestors for `display`/`visibility`/`opacity`. Baselined per viewport via
`replica.baseline.json` → `duplicateVisibleText`.
Proven both directions: silent on the fixed build; reports x2 for 5 headings
when the visibility filter is disabled (i.e. the bug state).

## THE BIG LESSON (I got this wrong twice in one session)
**Counting nodes/attributes is not evidence.** coframe.com itself keeps 12
`opacity:0` overlay clones and 2 `.cursor` clones permanently in its DOM. So:
- After the fix, local *still* showed "12 overlay clones, 6 duplicate headings"
  and I wrongly concluded the fix had failed and invented a second
  "runtime port bug in coframeCursorAnimation.ts" that **did not exist**.
- The decisive measurement is **visible** duplication, run **identically on the
  live site**, with live as the arbiter.
- Final proof: local and live are byte-identical — hero string 1-in-DOM/1-visible
  both; `We outperform both SaaS and CRO agencies.` and `Sharing our knowledge`
  2-in-DOM/**0-visible** both; `.cursor` bubbles 2-in-DOM/**0-visible** both.
- Also: check the **live runtime DOM**, not just the generated JSX. Clean JSX
  does not by itself prove a clean render.

## Gate results after the fix
- `npm run verify` exit 0 (tsc + 34/34 vitest + next build 4/4 pages)
- `npm run viewports` PASS 0 problems / 7 viewports, 47/48 animations, 2 carousels
- `npm run compare` avg **0.59%** across 7 viewports, heights identical on 6/7
